name: Transaxillary breast augmentation

card.summary: A breast implant operation done through a small incision in the armpit, so that implants add breast volume without a scar on the breast itself.
card.aka: armpit approach; TABA; endoscopic transaxillary augmentation
card.note: Surgical procedure with general operative and implant-related risks; performed by licensed surgeons only.

quick.overview:
Transaxillary breast augmentation places a breast implant through an incision in the armpit crease. The implant is guided under the skin to a pocket behind the breast, so the visible result is a fuller chest contour while the breast skin is left without an incision scar.

Surgical reviews describe it as especially popular in East Asia, and report outcomes comparable to the more common inframammary approach when an endoscope is used to give the surgeon a direct view of the pocket. Randomized and comparative trials have looked at endoscopic versus blind techniques and at different pocket planes.
quick.how: It is performed in an operating room under anesthesia by a plastic surgeon. A short armpit incision is made, a pocket is created for the implant (often with an endoscope for visualization), and the implant is placed and the incision closed. Patients choosing it typically do so because they prefer to avoid a scar on the breast; surgeons consider breast shape, the position of the breast crease and implant type when choosing an approach.
quick.risks: As with other breast augmentation approaches, risks include bleeding, infection, implant malposition or asymmetry, capsular contracture and later reoperation. Axillary-specific issues reported in the literature include armpit scarring, bowstring-like cords (Mondor's disease) and possible interaction with later sentinel lymph node mapping for breast cancer. Surgeons differ on how it compares technically with other approaches.

lead: Transaxillary breast augmentation is a method of placing breast implants through an incision in the armpit instead of at the breast crease, around the areola, or at the navel. The implant is tunneled to a pocket beneath the breast, either by blunt dissection or, in modern practice, under direct endoscopic vision [3][4]. It is one of the standard incision choices for breast augmentation alongside the inframammary, periareolar and transumbilical approaches [17].

People choose it to increase breast volume and change chest contour while avoiding a scar on the breast. Plastic surgery reviews describe the axillary route as the most common incision among Korean women and the favoured one among many Asian patients, and as a good option for young patients with an indistinct inframammary fold who want to avoid a chest scar [1][2].

Research on the technique consists mainly of surgeon-authored reviews, case series and a few randomized trials comparing endoscopic with non-endoscopic technique or comparing pocket planes. Authors who advocate it argue that endoscopic assistance gives control equal to other approaches [4]; other papers discuss specific drawbacks such as axillary scarring, implant malposition and sentinel node mapping [5][9][18]. The randomized evidence on endoscopic assistance is mixed: a 2015 trial found longer operations without better outcomes [8], while a 2026 trial reported fewer complications with video assistance [7].

angle.text: The implant itself adds breast volume; the armpit route changes where the scar sits. People who choose it do so to keep the incision out of the breast area, where it would show in swimwear or low necklines.

paras: In the transaxillary approach the surgeon makes a short incision in the armpit, tunnels the implant across under the skin and creates a pocket either above or below the pectoral muscle, beneath the fascia, or in a dual plane. Reviews note that the technique can be done by hand or with an endoscope [17][3].

Wikipedia's overview of incision options describes the inframammary cut as giving the surgeon the most access at the cost of a longer scar at the crease, the periareolar cut as roughly 5 cm along the areola's edge with higher reported contracture risk and possible effects on milk ducts and nerves, and the transaxillary route as avoiding breast-skin scars with symmetric placement as its main technical challenge [17]. It also describes incisions that avoid the nipple-areola complex, including the transaxillary, as helping preserve sensation and breastfeeding [17].

Endoscopic assistance is described as allowing a bloodless pocket and sharp dissection under direct vision. A 2014 Korean review describes electrocautery dissection under endoscopic view with round textured or anatomical cohesive gel implants, noting that texture adheres to tissue and helps define the inframammary crease [2]. A 2023 review by a Chinese surgeon presents a freestyle endoscopic technique with high-position dual-plane placement and says Asian patients typically favour the axillary incision [1].

Wikipedia traces the silicone-gel implant to plastic surgeons Frank Gerow and Thomas Cronin, with first augmentation use in 1962 and a French saline-filled implant presented in 1964. Later generations brought thicker shells and more cohesive gels intended to reduce leakage, and the structured saline implant was approved in 2014 and later discontinued [17].

The pocket may be subglandular (between breast tissue and muscle), subfascial, subpectoral or dual plane, or fully submuscular. Wikipedia lists the subglandular plane as giving a natural result but more rippling in thin tissue, and submuscular placement as having more pain and longer recovery but lower contracture rates and better coverage, with a risk of animation deformity where the implant moves with the muscle [17].

Historically the approach was perceived as offering less technical control. Authors of recent reviews argue that endoscopic assistance lets outcomes match those of the inframammary approach and that concerns about longer operations and higher contracture have been misunderstood [3][4]. One author describes the transaxillary route as widely seen as less controllable and sets out technical steps and postoperative measures intended to keep the implant in position [3].

A retrospective comparison of 78 women who had submuscular augmentation through the inframammary or the endoscopic transaxillary route between 1997 and 2004 found a low complication rate in both groups, with higher reported satisfaction in the transaxillary group [10]. A five-year retrospective study of 373 patients with form-stable textured implants compared transaxillary (302 patients) with periareolar (71) placement and found no statistically significant overall difference in reoperation, 8.3 percent versus 11 percent, though reoperation was significantly higher with the periareolar subfascial technique; grade III or IV contracture accounted for 3.3 and 4.2 percent respectively [14].

A prospective randomized study of 34 women compared transaxillary augmentation with and without video-assisted endoscopy using high-profile silicone implants in the subglandular plane, with about 25 months of follow-up. Operating time was longer with endoscopy, and the authors concluded it did not improve safety or aesthetic results [8]. A 2026 randomized trial of 118 patients enrolled between 2019 and 2022 compared a semiendoscopic video-assisted technique with the blind technique and reported longer operations but fewer complications, including asymmetry such as bottoming out and double-bubble deformity, animation deformity and capsular contracture [7].

A prospective randomized comparison of 53 women (2004 to 2005) examined subglandular, subfascial and submuscular implant placement through the axilla with textured silicone implants. Axillary incision complications occurred in 9 percent, satisfaction was similar across planes at 6 months and 3 years, and the authors suggested the subfascial plane combined advantages of the other two [9].

Case series include a 1996 to 2005 review of 306 endoscopic transaxillary patients using a 4 to 5 cm incision, with 3 hematomas, 5 capsular contractures, 1 infection and a 6.2 percent reoperation rate for malposition [11]; a series of 42 subfascial augmentations without an endoscope with 93 percent satisfied or very satisfied and 26 percent having an axillary-incision complication [18]; and a review of 197 endoscopic augmentations with saline implants in which careful patient selection was emphasised and 3.5 percent required revision for malposition [19]. Registered trials include a dual-plane axillary approach assisted by endoscope [15] and a study of anesthesia and recovery quality after transaxillary endoscopic augmentation [16].

General breast augmentation risks listed by Wikipedia include anesthesia reactions, hematoma, seroma, infection, pain, altered sensation, asymmetry, capsular contracture, rupture and symmastia, with later reoperation common [17]. Implants are regulated as Class III medical devices in the US, and in 2019 the FDA recalled Allergan Biocell textured implants over a link to breast implant-associated anaplastic large-cell lymphoma [17]. Wikipedia reports that reviews found no causal link between implants and systemic autoimmune disease, although many women report symptoms [17].

Specific to the axillary route, a 2007 review raised that more rigid cohesive-gel implants could traumatize the armpit and interfere with sentinel node mapping in a later breast cancer [5], while a single-patient case report and a lymphatic drainage study reported that sentinel node detection was feasible after transaxillary augmentation [12][13]. A case report with a literature review described Mondor's disease, a rare self-limiting subcutaneous cord that can follow surgery, in the upper inner arm after transaxillary augmentation [6]. Axillary scarring such as hypertrophic scar or small wound dehiscence and inner-arm sensory change appear in several series [9][18].

timeline.event: Silicone-gel implants are first used for breast augmentation [17].
Start of a nine-year series of 306 endoscopic transaxillary augmentations [11].
Comparison of inframammary and endoscopic transaxillary submuscular augmentation; case report on sentinel node detection after transaxillary augmentation [10][13].
Registered trial of dual-plane axillary augmentation assisted by endoscope begins [15].
Review raises sentinel node mapping concerns with rigid gel implants via the axilla [5]; 306-patient series published [11].
Randomized comparison of subglandular, subfascial and submuscular placement through the axilla [9].
Korean review describes fully endoscopic transaxillary augmentation as comparable to inframammary results [2].
Randomized trial finds video-assisted endoscopy lengthens transaxillary operations [8].
Five-year outcomes of form-stable implants via periareolar and transaxillary routes published [14].
FDA-announced recall of Allergan Biocell textured implants over BIA-ALCL [17].
Review presents freestyle endoscopic transaxillary technique with high-position dual plane [1].
Randomized trial compares semiendoscopic video-assisted and blind transaxillary techniques [7].
